title: Curve Sketching: Connecting f, f', and f''
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: Curve sketching combines f, f', and f'': the first derivative gives direction and extrema, the second derivative gives concavity and inflection points.
f'(x) > 0 means the graph is increasing, f'(x) < 0 means decreasing, and f'(x) = 0 means a horizontal tangent.
f''(x) > 0 means concave up and f''(x) < 0 means concave down.
Direction and concavity combine into four local shapes: increasing concave up, increasing concave down, decreasing concave down, and decreasing concave up.
Increasing and concave up means rising and steepening; increasing and concave down means rising but leveling off toward a peak.
Decreasing and concave down means falling and steepening downward; decreasing and concave up means falling but flattening toward a valley.
The curve-sketching checklist covers domain, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes, first-derivative analysis, and second-derivative analysis.
For the domain, watch for division by zero, even roots of negative numbers, and logarithms of non-positive numbers.
Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) and are symmetric about the y-axis; odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) and are symmetric about the origin.
For rational functions, find vertical asymptotes where the denominator is zero and horizontal asymptotes from the behavior as x approaches positive or negative infinity.
Example: for f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1, f'(x) = 3(x − 1)(x − 3) gives a local max at (1, 5) and local min at (3, 1).
For that function, f''(x) = 6(x − 2) gives an inflection point at (2, 3), concave down before x = 2 and concave up after.
A complete sketch plots extrema, inflection points, and intercepts, then connects them with a smooth curve matching the sign of f' and f'' on every interval.
A zero of f' or f'' is only a candidate; an extremum needs f' to change sign and an inflection point needs f'' to change sign.
Sketching from f' alone is insufficient because concavity from f'' is needed to get the correct bending of the curve.
When given the graph of f', the height of f' is the slope of f and the slope of f' is the concavity of f.
Where the f' graph is above the x-axis f is increasing, and where it crosses zero from positive to negative f has a local maximum.
Where the f' graph is rising, f is concave up; where the f' graph has a local maximum or minimum, f has an inflection point.
Example: given f'(x) = x(x − 2)(x + 1) and f(0) = 3, f has local minima at x = −1 and x = 2 and a local maximum at (0, 3).
The most common sketching error from an f' graph is treating it as the graph of f, leading to reversed conclusions about increase and concavity.
A complete sketch of a rational function must include asymptotes and end behavior, not just interior extrema.
Reconstructing f from f' is qualitative in differentiation but becomes quantitative in integration, where the integral of f' recovers f up to a constant via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
